strengths: Timely and practically motivated problem: Test-time scaling (TTS) in robot manipulation is typically reliant on external value functions or reward models (e.g., RoboMonkey), which are costly to train, deploy, and often fail to generalize. Proposing an intrinsic, verifier-free selection mechanism is valuable.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is validated across multiple simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, and CALVIN), multiple VLA architectures (π0-FAST, OpenVLA, MiniVLA), and physical robot experiments on a Franka Research 3 arm spanning in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks.

Practical deployment considerations: The paper addresses the inference overhead of parallel candidate generation by introducing a single-prefill deployment strategy, demonstrating concrete latency savings (e.g., 45% reduction at N=4).

Detailed ablation and analysis: Thorough ablations are provided covering candidate size N, regularization temperature, condition-masking variants, joint training effects, and the impact of action token truncation for the FAST tokenizer.
weaknesses: Nuance in the 'without additional training' claim: The abstract emphasizes that the framework operates 'without requiring additional training or external modules.' However, the strongest version of the method (MG-Select*) relies heavily on joint imitation learning with condition dropout. While training-free MG-Select yields improvements, they are noticeably smaller (e.g., 5.3% -> 7.2% vs. 14.2% on RoboCasa 30 demos), making the claim somewhat overstated.

Heuristic selection of masking modes and hyperparameters: The choice of which modality to mask (text vs. state vs. both) varies across benchmarks (e.g., state-masking works best for SIMPLER, text-masking for RoboCasa). Additionally, tuning hyperparameters such as the reference distribution regularization temperature (searching between 4.0 and 16.0) and token truncation length adds sensitivity that may require per-domain calibration.

Modest performance improvements on certain suites: On well-established saturated or long-horizon benchmarks like LIBERO with π0-FAST (Table 6), the overall gain is modest (92.0% -> 93.1%), with small regressions observed on LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal.

Conceptual novelty: The core idea builds directly on self-certainty and contrastive/unconditioned reference distributions from the LLM/diffusion literature (e.g., CFG and Kang et al., 2025). The adaptation to discrete action token distributions in autoregressive VLAs is neat and solid, but conceptually incremental.

strengths: Well-motivated and novel verifier-free test-time scaling method for VLAs: Adapting internal confidence/self-certainty mechanisms via condition-masking reference distributions eliminates the heavy overhead, task-specific reward engineering, and poor out-of-distribution transfer associated with external verifiers.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse benchmarks and model backbones: The method is validated on multiple simulation suites (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, CALVIN), across diverse architectures (π0-FAST, OpenVLA, MiniVLA), and on a physical Franka robot platform under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution conditions.

Practical efficiency and deployment focus: The proposed single-prefill optimization amortizes the visual/language prefill computation across candidate action decodings, achieving substantial latency reductions (e.g., ~45% speedup at N=4) and making test-time sampling feasible for closed-loop robotic control.

Thorough ablations and insights into action tokenization: The ablations thoughtfully analyze candidate count N, regularization temperature, dropout ratios, and action token aggregation schemes (providing valuable analysis of low- vs. high-frequency token reconstruction for FAST tokenizers).
weaknesses: Condition-masking selection requires task-specific heuristic choices: As described in Section 3.2 and Appendix A.3, the optimal condition to mask differs depending on the benchmark (e.g., state-masking on SIMPLER-WidowX vs. text-masking on RoboCasa). In open-ended autonomous deployment, determining which modality to drop without ground-truth task validation remains challenging.

Performance degradation on high-accuracy atomic tasks: On benchmarks where the base policy is already near ceiling (e.g., LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal in Table 6), stochastic sampling and selection can introduce noise and slightly degrade performance compared to greedy decoding.

Limited exploration of non-verifier baseline selectors: While compared against likelihood, uniform-KL, and RoboMonkey, the paper would be strengthened by comparing against other natural test-time aggregation baselines such as continuous trajectory clustering / medoid selection (trajectory self-consistency) or beam search.

Theoretical contribution in Appendix E is standard: The derivation proving that temperature scaling monotonically increases softmax distribution entropy is a standard mathematical property of the Boltzmann/softmax distribution rather than a novel theoretical insight specific to this framework.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important challenge in Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs): overcoming the suboptimality of single-inference greedy decoding without relying on computationally expensive external verifiers or value functions.

The evaluation covers a wide range of settings, including multiple simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, and CALVIN in the appendix) and real-world robotic manipulation on a 7-DoF Franka robot across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks.
The single-prefill deployment optimization is practical and effectively mitigates the computational latency overhead typically associated with batch candidate generation in autoregressive VLAs.
The paper provides an extensive suite of ablations investigating sampling candidates, temperature scaling, masking modalities, and token aggregation schemes.
weaknesses: Discrepancy regarding the 'training-free' claim: The paper positions MG-Select as a test-time framework that requires no additional training, yet the best-performing variant (MG-Select*) relies on Joint Imitation Learning (condition dropout fine-tuning). Crucially, the ablation in Table 5(d) shows that Joint-IL alone accounts for the bulk of the gain (improving PnP success from 17.0% to 28.5%), while adding MG-Select on top only increases it to 31.0%. This suggests that the training-time regularization drives most of the improvement rather than test-time candidate selection.

Marginal gain over simple likelihood selection: Table 5(a) indicates that selecting candidate actions by predicted sequence likelihood achieves 30.5% (PnP) / 46.8% (All), whereas the proposed condition-masking KL metric achieves 31.0% (PnP) / 48.1% (All). The performance delta over standard log-likelihood Best-of-N reranking is quite small given the added complexity of computing masked forward passes.

Extensive per-benchmark test-time hyperparameter tuning: Appendix A.3 notes that multiple key hyperparameters—including sampling temperature, masking modality (text, state, or both), reference regularization temperature (ranging from 4.0 to 16.0), and token aggregation window—are tuned individually for each dataset. This extensive per-task tuning raises concerns regarding test-set overfitting and deployment brittleness when faced with truly novel tasks.

Ad-hoc aggregation strategy tied to tokenizer specifics: The token aggregation method relies heavily on heuristic truncation (e.g., first 5 tokens for FAST on RoboCasa, first 1 token on SIMPLER, and full averaging for OpenVLA). The lack of a unified, principled criterion for aggregating sequence-level divergence limits the generalizability of the scoring rule across architectures.

Scope limited to discrete autoregressive VLAs: The theoretical and practical formulation strictly relies on categorical distributions over discrete action tokens, making the framework inapplicable to popular diffusion- or flow-matching-based continuous action policies (e.g., standard π0, Octo, Diffusion Policy) without major architectural rework.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge in robotics: scaling test-time compute for autoregressive Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models without relying on separate reward models, external verifiers, or reinforcement learning critics.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO) and physical robot hardware (Franka Research 3), testing both in-distribution and out-of-distribution generalization.

Good coverage of ablation studies, analyzing candidate set size, masking configurations, sampling temperatures, token aggregation strategies, and inference strategies against simpler baselines (greedy, random sampling, uniform KL, likelihood).
Addresses practical deployment considerations by demonstrating that a single-prefill optimization across candidates substantially mitigates parallel generation latency.
weaknesses: The performance margin over simpler test-time selection baselines is relatively modest. In Table 5(a), MG-Select achieves 31.0% / 48.1% on RoboCasa (PnP / All), compared to 30.5% / 46.8% for standard token likelihood selection and 30.0% / 46.5% for uniform KL divergence.

A significant portion of the reported improvement stems from the joint training strategy (condition dropout) rather than test-time sampling itself. As shown in Table 5(d), joint training alone boosts the base policy from 17.0% to 28.5% on PnP, whereas adding MG-Select on top accounts for a +2.5% increment.

High sensitivity to hyperparameter tuning: the method requires selecting task-specific condition-masking variants (e.g., state-masking for SIMPLER vs. text-masking for RoboCasa), token truncation ranges (first 5 tokens for FAST vs. full average for OpenVLA), and high reference regularization temperatures (searched over {4.0 to 16.0}). Grid-searching and picking the best configuration per benchmark raises concerns about hyperparameter transferability in real-world deployment.
Mixed performance on some task suites: on LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal (Table 6), MG-Select slightly degrades success rates compared to the base model for both OpenVLA and π0-FAST.

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: Addresses the test-time scaling bottleneck in autoregressive Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models without requiring external verifiers or value-function training.

Comprehensive evaluation: Evaluates across multiple standard simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO) and validates on real-world Franka robot manipulation tasks across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution conditions.
Demonstrated cross-architecture applicability: Validates the core approach across two distinct autoregressive VLA models (π0-FAST and OpenVLA).

Detailed ablation and systems analysis: Thoroughly ablates key design choices (sampling temperature, number of candidates, masking variants, aggregation methods) and introduces an efficient single-prefill deployment strategy to mitigate inference latency.
weaknesses: Per-benchmark hyperparameter tuning: Appendix A.3 indicates that hyperparameters (sampling temperature, number of candidates, masking variant, and reference distribution regularization temperature) were grid-searched per benchmark to report the best result, rather than selected on a separate validation set. This raises concerns regarding hyperparameter sensitivity and potential test-set overfitting.

Disentanglement of joint training versus test-time selection: Table 5(d) shows that joint training (Joint-IL) alone accounts for the dominant share of the performance gain on RoboCasa (17.0% to 28.5% on Pick and Place), whereas adding MG-Select yields a much smaller incremental gain (28.5% to 31.0%). Clarifying whether MG-Select's value is primarily due to data regularization during fine-tuning or test-time filtering is important.

Marginal improvement over simpler test-time heuristics: As shown in Table 5(a), standard likelihood-based Best-of-N selection already achieves 30.5% (PnP) / 46.8% (All), and uniform KL divergence achieves 30.0% / 46.5%, compared to MG-Select's 31.0% / 48.1%. The margin gained by condition-masking KL divergence over simple likelihood is relatively small.

Mixed results on LIBERO benchmark: On LIBERO (Table 6), the overall gains are minor (e.g., +1.6% for OpenVLA and +1.1% for π0-FAST), and performance actually regresses on two of the four suites (LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal).

Decoding computational overhead: Because the reference distribution requires running the model under masked inputs conditioned on the same candidate action prefix, computing token-wise KL divergence requires additional forward passes during autoregressive generation that are not fully reflected in the prefill analysis.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in robot manipulation: enabling test-time compute/scaling for Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) without requiring external verifiers or reward models.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning three major simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO) as well as physical experiments on a 7-DoF Franka Research 3 robot arm across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings.
Careful engineering consideration for inference latency via a shared single-prefill deployment strategy that mitigates the computational bottleneck of parallel Best-of-N generation.
Extensive ablation studies analyzing inference strategies, candidate counts, temperature regularization, condition masking choices, and token aggregation schemes.
weaknesses: Confounding between test-time scaling and training-time data augmentation: The proposed joint training strategy (Joint-IL with condition dropout) accounts for a large portion of the overall performance improvement. In Table 5(d), moving from vanilla IL to Joint-IL alone improves pick-and-place success from 17.0% to 28.5%, whereas adding MG-Select on top yields a much smaller increment (from 28.5% to 31.0%). This blurs the paper's core positioning as a purely test-time scaling solution.

Mixed performance and regressions on standard benchmarks: On the LIBERO benchmark (Table 6), the overall gains are modest (+1.6% for OpenVLA, +1.1% for π0-FAST), and performance actually degrades on multiple sub-suites (e.g., OpenVLA drops from 85.2% to 81.7% on LIBERO-Spatial and 75.5% to 73.6% on LIBERO-Goal; π0-FAST drops from 95.6% to 94.5% on LIBERO-Goal). This undermines the claim that MG-Select consistently improves base models across diverse tasks.

Narrow margin over standard likelihood selection: In Table 5(a), simple Best-of-N selection using sequence likelihood achieves 46.8% overall success compared to 48.1% for MG-Select (and 46.5% for uniform KL). The empirical benefit of the condition-masking KL formulation over basic likelihood or uniform uncertainty baselines is relatively marginal.

High sensitivity and heavy hyperparameter tuning: As described in Appendix A.3, applying the method requires tuning multiple hyperparameters per dataset/model—including the choice of masked modality (text, state, or both), high regularization temperatures (ranging from 4.0 to 16.0), and token index aggregation ranges (e.g., first 5 tokens for π0-FAST vs. full average for OpenVLA, where summing or averaging all tokens on π0-FAST underperforms greedy decoding in Table 5(f)). This lack of a unified, robust setting reduces practical usability on new downstream tasks.

Conceptual limitation of the token-wise KL confidence: The KL divergence KL(Q_i || P_i) measures the distributional discrepancy between conditional and unconditional distributions given prefix a_{<i}; it does not evaluate the probability or quality of the candidate token a_i itself. The theoretical rationale for why prefix divergence serves as an effective action-selection verifier could be formalized more rigorously.
